item.title: Elder Kulla: Kulla went to the charnel ground, Saw a woman abandoned, Thrown away in the cemetery, Food for worms. “Kulla, look at this body…
item.description:
Elder Kulla:

Kulla went to the charnel ground,
Saw a woman abandoned,
Thrown away in the cemetery,
Food for worms.

“Kulla, look at this body —
Diseased, foul, stinking,
Oozing, seeping,
Delighting fools.”

Having taken up the mirror of Dhamma,
I attained right view.
I contemplated this body —
Empty inside and out.

As it is below, so above,
As above, so below,
As below, so above,
As above, so below.

As by day, so by night,
As by night, so by day,
As before, so after,
As after, so before.

Such a one does not delight
In the five kinds of music.
When one-pointed,
Rightly meditating on the Dhamma.

From: Theragāthā 6.4

item.title: “And how, monks, is dwelling heedfully? If one lives with restraint of the eye faculty, monks, his mind is not defiled by forms cognizable by…
item.description:
“And how, monks, is dwelling heedfully? If one lives with restraint of the eye faculty, monks, his mind is not defiled by forms cognizable by the eye. For one with an undefiled mind, gladness arises. With gladness, rapture arises. With rapture, the body becomes tranquil. With a tranquil body, he experiences ease. For one at ease, the mind becomes concentrated. When the mind is concentrated, phenomena are clearly seen. When phenomena are clearly seen, he is called ‘one who dwells heedfully’ … the ear faculty … the nose faculty … the tongue faculty … the body faculty … If one lives with restraint of the mind faculty, his mind is not defiled by phenomena cognizable by the mind. For one with an undefiled mind, gladness arises … he is called ‘one who dwells heedfully.’ Thus, monks, is dwelling heedfully.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.97

item.title: “Furthermore, wanderers, a brahmin says: ‘All sensual pleasures are impermanent, suffering, subject to change.’ That brahmin speaks truth, not falsehood. And by directly knowing the…
item.description:
“Furthermore, wanderers, a brahmin says: ‘All sensual pleasures are impermanent, suffering, subject to change.’ That brahmin speaks truth, not falsehood. And by directly knowing the truth contained therein, he practices disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding sensual pleasures.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.185

item.title: (The Blessed One): I am freed From Māra’s trap, Freed from the bonds of sensual pleasures, Both heavenly and human. I am freed From Māra’s…
item.description:
(The Blessed One):
I am freed
From Māra’s trap,
Freed from the bonds of sensual pleasures,
Both heavenly and human.
I am freed
From Māra’s fetter.
O Death, you are
Defeated.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.4
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, one who delights in forms delights in suffering. One who delights in suffering, I say, is not freed from suffering. One who delights in…
item.description:
“Monks, one who delights in forms delights in suffering. One who delights in suffering, I say, is not freed from suffering. One who delights in sounds … in odors … in tastes … in touches … One who delights in phenomena delights in suffering. One who delights in suffering, I say, is not freed from suffering. One who does not delight in forms, monks, does not delight in suffering. One who does not delight in suffering, I say, is freed from suffering. One who does not delight in sounds … odors … tastes … touches … One who does not delight in phenomena does not delight in suffering. One who does not delight in suffering, I say, is freed from suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.20

item.title: - What binds the world? What leads the world? By abandoning what thing Is Nibbāna called? - Delight binds the world, Seeking leads the world,…
item.description:
- What binds the world?
What leads the world?
By abandoning what thing
Is Nibbāna called?
- Delight binds the world,
Seeking leads the world,
By abandoning craving,
Is Nibbāna called.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.64

item.title: “Monks, there are these three things. What three? Sensual thought, ill-will thought, harmful thought. Monks, these are the three things. To abandon these three things,…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these three things. What three? Sensual thought, ill-will thought, harmful thought. Monks, these are the three things. To abandon these three things, three things should be developed. What three? To abandon sensual thought, the thought of renunciation should be developed. To abandon ill-will thought, the thought of non-ill-will should be developed. To abandon harmful thought, the thought of harmlessness should be developed. To abandon those three things, monks, these three things should be developed.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.109

item.title: “Mind precedes all mental states, Mind is their chief; they are all mind-made. If with an impure mind one speaks or acts, Suffering follows like…
item.description:
“Mind precedes all mental states,
Mind is their chief; they are all mind-made.
If with an impure mind one speaks or acts,
Suffering follows like the wheel that follows the ox’s foot.”

“Mind precedes all mental states,
Mind is their chief; they are all mind-made.
If with a pure mind one speaks or acts,
Happiness follows like a shadow that never leaves.”

From: Dhammapada 1-20

item.title: “Venerable sirs, what is the effort of abandoning? Here, a monk does not consent to arisen sensual thought; he abandons, dispels, destroys, makes it non-existent.…
item.description:
“Venerable sirs, what is the effort of abandoning? Here, a monk does not consent to arisen sensual thought; he abandons, dispels, destroys, makes it non-existent. He does not consent to arisen ill-will thought … he does not consent to arisen harmful thought; he abandons, dispels, destroys, makes it non-existent. This, venerable sirs, is called the effort of abandoning.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 33 – Saṅgītisutta

item.title: Then the Venerable Ānanda went to that nun, sat down on the prepared seat, and said to her: “Sister, this body is produced by food,…
item.description:
Then the Venerable Ānanda went to that nun, sat down on the prepared seat, and said to her: “Sister, this body is produced by food, depends on food. Food should be abandoned. Sister, this body is produced by craving, depends on craving. Craving should be abandoned. Sister, this body is produced by conceit, depends on conceit. Conceit should be abandoned. Sister, this body is produced by sexual intercourse, depends on sexual intercourse. Sexual intercourse — the breaking of the bridge — has been spoken of by the Blessed One. ‘Sister, this body is produced by food, depends on food. Food should be abandoned.’ Thus it has been said. For what reason was this said?”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.159
